source: Capacities are rounded from the NASA Launch Services Program Launch Vehicle Performance site (https://elvperf.ksc.nasa.gov) and the vendors' public payload user guides and capability pages; prices from public list prices and NASA contract announcements. Approximate values for gameplay, not for mission planning.
units: cost_musd in millions of US dollars. c3_capacity is [launch energy C3 in km^2/s^2, payload in kg]. sso_capacity is [circular altitude in km, payload in kg] to sun-synchronous orbit. reliability is the probability of a successful launch.

vehicles.name: Rideshare slot
vehicles.summary: A seat on a big rocket carrying dozens of small satellites: by far the cheapest way up. Everyone gets off near 525 km, so a higher orbit costs most of the seat to a transfer stage.

vehicles.name: Electron
vehicles.summary: Dedicated small launcher: you choose the orbit and the date, but it lifts only a couple of hundred kilograms and cannot leave Earth orbit with a lander.

vehicles.name: Alpha
vehicles.summary: Three times Electron's lift for twice the price, with a shorter flight record: more room for payload, more launch risk.

vehicles.name: Falcon 9 (booster recovered)
vehicles.summary: The workhorse: very reliable and cheap per kilogram. Its lift drops quickly as the launch energy rises, so heavy designs and fast transfers outgrow it.

vehicles.name: Vulcan Centaur VC2
vehicles.summary: A high-energy upper stage keeps more of its lift on escape trajectories than Falcon 9, for a higher price.

vehicles.name: Atlas V 541
vehicles.summary: The rocket that launched Curiosity and Perseverance: a flawless record at a premium price.

vehicles.name: Falcon Heavy (expendable)
vehicles.summary: Three boosters thrown away for one launch: it forgives a heavy design, and the bill shows it.

vehicles.name: Space Launch System Block 1
vehicles.summary: The most powerful rocket flying. It lifts anything, and costs more than most whole missions.
